passage: Selin had been working at a café in Istanbul while finishing university. For months she slept badly, skipped meals and said "fine" when anyone asked. She stopped going to her Friday dance class. Her friend Rafael noticed she hadn't laughed in weeks. One evening he found her sitting in the storeroom, staring at the shelves. "I don't feel anything," she said. "I'm tired all the time and nothing seems worth it." Rafael sat with her. "That sounds heavy. Would you talk to someone? The university has a counsellor." She shrugged, but he helped her book an appointment on his phone right there. The next week she went. She said afterwards it was strange but a relief to say it all out loud.

qa.a: She stopped going to her Friday dance class.

qa.q: What does Selin's "I don't feel anything" suggest about her state?
qa.a: It suggests she was deeply exhausted and emotionally numb, and had lost hope, which are warning signs to take seriously.

qa.q: What made Rafael's response helpful?
qa.a: He listened without judging and helped her book a counsellor appointment immediately, turning concern into a concrete step.

qa.q: How might Rafael feel after Selin went to the counsellor?
qa.a: He might feel relieved and hopeful, but also keep checking on her since recovery takes time. 🤍

Week one of finals prep. Keerthana stopped going to the evening badminton she had played for three years. "No time," she told Kamal. She slept eleven hours on Sunday and still woke tired.
Three weeks later. She hadn't answered her mother's calls in four days. The notes she used to colour-code sat unopened. When Kamal knocked with dinner, she said through the door, "What's the point? I'll fail anyway." Kamal didn't leave. He sat outside and said, "This isn't laziness. It's been weeks. Will you come with me to the counselling centre tomorrow at ten? I'll wait outside."
Five weeks later. Keerthana had seen the counsellor twice and a doctor once. Some days she was still tired. But she had called her mother back, and on Friday she picked up her racket and played one slow game.

subtype: Recognizing Warning Signs & Seeking Professional Help
passage: Tenzin, you keep saying you're "just tired". Let me, your old Urmila Didi from the ward, tell you something. When I was twenty-two I was a staff nurse in my first year, taking double shifts because I thought saying no meant I was weak. For two months I stopped eating proper meals. I stopped going to my friend Leela's for Sunday lunch. I cried in the linen room and told myself everyone does. One morning I stood at the trolley and couldn't remember why I was there. My matron, a stern woman called Mrs Gomes, took me into her office. She didn't scold. She said, "This has gone on too long. You'll see the staff doctor today, and I'm taking you off doubles." I was ashamed then. Now I think she saved my career. So when you say "just tired" for the third month, I hear my younger self.

qa.q: Where did Urmila cry?
qa.a: In the linen room.

qa.q: What was young Urmila feeling when Mrs Gomes took her into the office?
qa.a: Urmila felt ashamed at the time, believing that needing help meant being weak.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Urmila's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Mrs Gomes stepped in that same day, sending Urmila to the staff doctor and ending double shifts, so help came early before things got worse.

subtype: Recognizing Warning Signs & Seeking Professional Help
passage:
In my first job, I worked until midnight for four months straight. I thought that was what ambitious people did.
Then my body started giving signals. Headaches every day. I stopped reading, stopped calling friends. I snapped at a junior for a tiny mistake and felt nothing afterwards.
My manager, Shalini, called me in. I thought I was in trouble. Instead she said, "You don't seem like yourself. Our company has a free counsellor. Would you talk to her?"
I was embarrassed. But I went. The counsellor helped me see it was burnout, not weakness. I started leaving at seven, taking walks, and seeing a doctor for the headaches.
I'm Lalit. I wish I'd asked for help at month one, not month four.

qa.q: How long did Lalit work until midnight?
qa.a: Four months straight.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling after snapping at the junior?
qa.a: Lalit felt numb, which itself was a warning sign of burnout.

qa.q: What choice helped Lalit recover?
qa.a: Accepting Shalini's suggestion to see the company counsellor, then changing work hours and seeing a doctor.

qa.q: How might Shalini have seen Lalit before calling Lalit in?
qa.a: Shalini likely noticed the changes with concern, not as a performance problem.

Thursday, 11 p.m.
It's Reena. I've been writing "tired" in this diary for two months. I counted tonight: fifty-three times.
It's not normal tired. I sleep ten hours and wake up heavy. I've stopped going to dance practice, which I used to love. I left the group chat on mute. I cry in the hostel bathroom and don't know why. When Manjula Aunty, my warden, asked if I was okay, I said "exams", even though exams finished two weeks ago.
The college health poster says: if low mood or exhaustion lasts more than two weeks, talk to someone. It's been eight.
So today I booked an appointment with the campus counsellor for tomorrow at ten. Then I went to Manjula Aunty's room and told her the truth. She made me tea and said she'll walk me there.
I'm scared. But I'm less alone than this morning.

qa.a: Fifty-three times.

qa.a: Reena feels scared about the appointment, but less alone than in the morning.

qa.a: The heavy tiredness, withdrawal and crying had lasted eight weeks, well beyond a bad patch, so early professional help matters.

qa.a: Manjula Aunty was probably concerned and a bit saddened she had missed it, but glad Reena trusted her and ready to help.
